problem: A projectile is launched at 20 m/s at 30° above horizontal from ground level. Take g = 10 m/s². Find (a) the time of flight, (b) the maximum height reached, and (c) the horizontal range.

steps.prompt: Decompose the launch velocity into horizontal and vertical components.
reveal: u_x = u · cos θ = 20 × cos 30° = 17.32 m/s
u_y = u · sin θ = 20 × sin 30° = 10 m/s

whyAnswers.question: Why do we need sin and cos at all?
whyAnswers.answer: Because the ball is not moving straight up — it is moving up AND forward at the same time. The angle (30°) is the only piece of information telling us how the 20 m/s is split between the two. Sin and cos are the geometric tools that perform that split for any right triangle. Without them, we cannot get H or R unless someone hands us the components directly.

whyAnswers.question: Can we avoid them for this specific question?
whyAnswers.answer: Only by remembering common values like sin 30° = 1/2 and cos 30° = √3/2. Then you can say 'at 30°, half the speed goes upward', giving u_y = 20 × 1/2 = 10 m/s without a calculator. But that is still using the result of sine — just from memory. There is no way to skip the split itself.

whyAnswers.question: Why can't I just use the full 20 m/s as the upward speed?
whyAnswers.answer: Because only a part of the velocity points upward. If you plug 20 m/s into H = u_y²/(2g), you get H = 400/20 = 20 m. But the real height is 5 m. The other 17.3 m/s is being spent moving forward, not gaining height. The ball doesn't get the benefit of its full speed in any single direction — it has to share.

whyAnswers.question: Why specifically sin and cos — why not some other tool?
whyAnswers.answer: Forget physics for a moment. Imagine a ladder leaning against a wall, 20 m long, making 30° with the floor. People worked out thousands of years ago that for any right triangle: cos θ = (horizontal side) / hypotenuse, sin θ = (vertical side) / hypotenuse. That is literally the definition of sin and cos — they were invented for this exact question. Your velocity arrow is just the ladder. Sin and cos are not extra physics — they are geometry that physics borrows.

steps.prompt: The horizontal motion has no acceleration. The vertical motion accelerates downward at g. Sketch the trajectory.
reveal: Horizontal: a_x = 0   →   u_x stays at 17.32 m/s.
Vertical:   a_y = −g  →   slows on the way up, speeds on the way down.

steps.prompt: At the highest point the vertical velocity is zero. Use v = u + a·t to find the time to reach the top.
By symmetry, the projectile takes the same time to come back down. So time of flight T = 2 · t_top.
Use v² = u² − 2·g·H at the highest point (where v = 0) to find the maximum height H.
The horizontal range is simply the horizontal speed times the total flight time. R = u_x · T.

finalAnswer: T = 2 s    H = 5 m    R ≈ 34.6 m
bonus: Shortcut formula:  R = u² · sin(2θ) / g  =  (20)² · sin 60° / 10  =  400 × 0.866 / 10  ≈  34.64 m
